opus-5.5.text:
Right, so this comes up whenever you want to do something iterative or recurrent, like a recurrent neural network, a Markov chain, or any dynamical system where you're updating a state over time.

The naive way to do it in TensorLogic would be to make time just another index. You'd have a state tensor indexed by, say, i for the units and t for the time step, and your equation would say that the state at t+1 is some function, a nonlinearity applied to a weight tensor times the state at t, summed over the shared index. That's perfectly well defined, and it's very clean mathematically. But the problem is that if you actually materialize that, you're storing the entire history of the state. For a long sequence that's wasteful, and most of the time you don't need it. You only care about the current state.

So the starred index is a way of saying: this index is virtual. You write the equation the same way, with State[i, *t+1] defined in terms of State[j, *t], but the star tells the system not to allocate a dimension for t. Instead, the tensor gets updated in place. Each time you apply the equation, the new value overwrites the old one. Semantically it's still the same equation, still a function of time, but operationally you're keeping only the current slice.

What I like about this is that it keeps the declarative character of the language. You're not suddenly writing a loop with assignment statements, which is how you'd do it in Python or PyTorch, and which breaks the nice correspondence between the program and the math. You still have one equation that says exactly what the relationship between successive states is. The star is just an annotation about how to store it. So it's a bit like the distinction in logic programming between the logical meaning of a program and its control: you separate what you're computing from how you're computing it.

And it generalizes. Anything with that flavor, whether it's message passing iterations, fixed-point computations, or forward chaining in a rule-based system until nothing changes, you can express with a virtual index, and you get constant memory in that dimension instead of linear. If at some point you do want the history, say for backpropagation through time, you just drop the star and the index becomes real again. It's a one-character change rather than a rewrite of the program, and that's the kind of thing I think a language for AI should make easy.

r001.rationale: It says the starred time index is virtual and is not allocated as a tensor dimension, so only the state index i remains as a storage dimension.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says each iteration’s new value overwrites the old value.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so this is one of the things I'm most excited about in Tensor Logic, because it's where the logic side and the neural side really start to pay off together. The basic idea is that in Tensor Logic everything is a tensor equation, and a tensor equation is also a rule in the Datalog sense. So if you want to represent something that changes over time, the natural way to do it is to give the tensor an index for time. You'd write something like State of t plus one is some function of State of t and the input at t. That's just a rule where the head has the next time step and the body has the current one.

Now, the problem is that if you literally materialize that, you have a tensor with a time dimension that grows unboundedly, and most of the time you don't actually care about the whole history. You care about the current state, and maybe you need the previous one to compute it. That's what the star is for. A starred index is an index that gets elided, if you will. It says: don't keep all the values of this dimension around, just keep the latest one, and when the equation fires, overwrite it. So State star is the current state, and the equation State star equals f of State star, Input star is read as: the new value of the state is a function of the old value. It's the same as the assignment with the arrow that you have in an ordinary programming language, except that it's still a tensor equation, so it still has all the properties we want. It's differentiable, you can learn it, you can reason over it.

And the nice thing is this gives you all the familiar things in one shot. A recurrent neural network is just a tensor equation with a starred index on the hidden state. The weight update in gradient descent is a tensor equation with a starred index on the weights. A loop in a program, a transition in a Markov chain, a step of a planner, those are all the same thing. So you don't need a separate construct for iteration or for state, you just need to mark which index you're not going to keep. And conceptually, you can always think of the starred version as a shorthand for the fully indexed one where the time dimension is explicit, so nothing semantically new is being added. It's purely a matter of what you choose to store, which in the end is what distinguishes a state from a history.

r001.rationale: The response says a starred index stores only the latest value, but it does not state that starring J in M_{IJ} leaves I as the storage dimension.

r002.rationale: It says the starred dimension keeps only the latest value and that each equation firing overwrites it, describing successive iterations replacing prior results.

astra-6.text: You use the starred index to distinguish successive versions of the state. So instead of writing a rule that looks as though the state depends on itself at the same instant, you write something like \(S_{t^*+1}=F(S_{t^*},X_t)\). You supply an initial state, and each application of the rule produces the next one. That lets you express an evolving computation—a recurrent network, for example—as a rule over a tensor with an explicit evolution index.

r001.rationale: The response describes a starred index for successive state versions, but does not mention starring J in M_{IJ} or that only I remains as the storage dimension.

r002.rationale: It says each rule application produces the next state, but does not state that successive iterations overwrite results stored by preceding iterations.

sol-6.1.text: You use the starred index to mark the dimension along which the state evolves. Think of a state tensor indexed by time: the update rule takes the state at one step and produces the state at the next. You can apply that same rule repeatedly, so the evolving state is represented by successive slices of the tensor, rather than by overwriting a single value.

r001.rationale: It describes a starred index as the evolving dimension, but does not state that starring J in M_{IJ} on the left-hand side leaves only I as a storage dimension.

r002.rationale: It says the evolving state is represented by successive slices rather than overwriting a single value, which does not communicate that iterations overwrite preceding results.
